title: Trump Declares Hormuz 'US Territory' and Threatens Indefinite Blockade; Asian Refiners Pivot to US Crude as Russia Tightens Grip on EU LNG
subhead: Washington escalated the Hormuz standoff from blockade to territorial claim — Trump says the US will 'keep' the strait and Hegseth vows an indefinite naval blockade plus unprecedented sanctions — while Asian refiners locked in US crude cargoes and Russia solidified its position as the EU's second-largest LNG supplier.

sections.heading: Trump Claims Hormuz as 'US Territory' as Hegseth Vows Indefinite Blockade
sections.body:
The US-Iran standoff over the Strait of Hormuz took a sharp rhetorical and operational escalation this week. President Trump wrote on Truth Social that 'I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT' regarding the strait, and told reporters the waterway would soon be 'called a territory of the United States,' according to CBS News and Mathrubhumi. Tehran responded that the strait is 'under Iran's control and management' (Yahoo News/CBS).

On the operational side, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the US Navy can maintain its naval blockade of Iran 'indefinitely' — 'we'll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we'll continue to' — and promised 'measures like have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country,' with announcements coming next week (Reuters, via OilPrice). Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent echoed the threat of economic isolation 'like the world has never seen before' (CBS News).

Meanwhile, tanker traffic through Hormuz kept sliding: only five crossings on Wednesday and nine on Thursday, down from a monthly average of 12, per Kpler data cited by Reuters — most of them moving along the Iranian corridor.
sections.whyItMatters: A US claim to 'keep' the strait as territory, paired with an indefinite blockade, marks a qualitative shift from a wartime disruption to a permanent US assertion of control over the world's most important oil chokepoint. It hardens Iran's position and pushes any diplomatic reopening further away, while the traffic data shows the physical market is already operating at a fraction of normal.

sections.heading: Asian Refiners Lock In US Crude as Hormuz Stays Closed
sections.body:
With Middle East crude effectively bottled up, Asian refiners moved decisively toward US barrels this week. Traders told Reuters that at least four Asia-based refiners bought US crude volumes, with the deals detailed by OilPrice: GS Caltex of South Korea bought 2 million barrels of Mars crude from Shell for November delivery at a premium of $13-14 above the Dubai benchmark; Japan's Cosmo Energy bought Mars from Trafigura; Eneos, Japan's largest refiner, bought 2 million barrels of WTI from Trafigura at a premium of over $10 above October WTI; and Taiwan's state-owned CPC acquired 2 million barrels of WTI at a premium of $8-9 to Dated Brent.

The buying comes as tight fuel markets and sky-high refining margins encourage refinery runs, and as Hormuz transit remains effectively closed. US commercial inventories added over 17.4 million barrels last week, per OilPrice, cushioning the domestic market even as global stocks deplete.
sections.whyItMatters: The premiums Asian refiners are paying — $8-14 over benchmark — quantify the cost of the Hormuz closure in real cargo terms. This is the market's own rerouting: US crude is becoming the default substitute for Gulf barrels, a shift that, if sustained, permanently reweights global crude trade flows toward the Atlantic basin.

sections.heading: Russia Solidifies Position as EU's Second-Largest LNG Supplier
sections.body:
Despite the EU's phased ban on Russian gas, Russia ranked second only to the US in the value of LNG supplied to the EU in June, with a 24.1% market share and purchases of approximately €809 million — a 57% increase year-on-year, according to TASS calculations based on Eurostat data. Belgium was the largest importer at €268 million, its highest figure since July 2025, followed by France (€258 million) and Spain (€201 million). The US led with a 54.3% share and €1.83 billion.

Russia also supplied €542 million of pipeline gas to the EU in June, a 12.5% share of pipeline imports, behind Norway (33.3%) and Algeria (23.6%). The EU's full ban on Russian LNG takes effect January 1, 2027, and on pipeline gas from September 30, 2027. In anticipation, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Russian companies would redirect LNG to China, India, Thailand and the Philippines without waiting for the EU ban (TASS).
sections.whyItMatters: The EU is still buying record volumes of Russian LNG even as it legislates a ban — a reminder that sanctions and market reality are running on different clocks. Russia is using the window to lock in alternative buyers in Asia, so the 2027 ban may cost Europe its leverage more than it costs Moscow its revenue.

sections.heading: Russia's Arctic Play: New Ice-Class LNG Carrier Heads Down the Northern Sea Route
sections.body:
Russia's second new domestically-built ice-class LNG carrier, the Konstantin Posiet, is heading via the Northern Sea Route, according to LSEG shipping data reported by Reuters. The move comes as China opens its first regular cargo route through the Arctic, with high oil prices and climate-driven ice retreat making the northern passage financially viable, per CNN and MSN.

The Moscow-controlled Northern Sea Route is increasingly cast as a new artery binding China and Russia together — Moscow needs the revenue and Beijing needs the energy, as Protothema's analysis of the CNN reporting put it. The route offers Russia an alternative export corridor that bypasses European and Hormuz-linked chokepoints entirely.
sections.whyItMatters: Every new ice-class carrier and Arctic cargo route is a brick in Russia's effort to decouple its energy exports from Western-controlled chokepoints. With Hormuz closed and European routes being sanctioned, the Northern Sea Route is becoming a strategic alternative that ties Russian energy more tightly to Chinese demand.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Launches Red Sea Maritime Defence Alliance; Pakistan Takes Deputy Command
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia has formally launched a multinational maritime defence coalition in the Red Sea, with 13 countries joining as members and representatives from 39 countries involved, according to Ilkha and MSN. Pakistan will provide the first deputy commander of the Saudi-led coalition, per ProPakistani, deepening Islamabad's role in Gulf security after its repeated mediation trips to Tehran.

The alliance comes as the Houthis continue to strike shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb strait — where traffic was in the double digits this week, with Kpler reporting 19 commodity carriers passing on Thursday — and as the Red Sea remains a contested corridor alongside the closed Hormuz.
sections.whyItMatters: A Saudi-led maritime alliance with Pakistani deputy command is a concrete security architecture forming in the Red Sea independent of the US. It signals that Gulf states are building their own protection for the one chokepoint that still carries traffic, even as the US focuses its naval power on Hormuz.

sections.heading: Oil Set for Weekly Gains as Stalled Talks Keep Risk Premium Alive
sections.body:
Oil futures were headed for weekly gains of around 5% as stalled talks to reopen Hormuz and persistent Gulf shipping risks kept the geopolitical premium embedded in prices, according to Dow Jones via Morningstar. September WTI closed up 1.42% on Friday, with RBOB gasoline also higher (Yahoo Finance). The gains came despite a large US inventory build, as traders weighed the indefinite-blockade threat against the demand-destruction forecasts from the IEA and OPEC earlier in the week.

US oil drillers added rigs this week, per Baker Hughes data cited by OilPrice, as higher prices incentivize domestic production.
sections.whyItMatters: The market is now caught between two forces: the supply-risk premium from an indefinite blockade and the demand-destruction drag from the IEA and OPEC forecasts. For now the supply side is winning, but the tension means prices are likely to stay volatile and range-bound until the Hormuz question resolves one way or the other.

bottomLine: The Hormuz standoff escalated from a wartime disruption into a US claim of permanent control: Trump says the US will 'keep' the strait, Hegseth vows an indefinite naval blockade and unprecedented sanctions, and Tehran insists the waterway remains under Iranian management — while tanker traffic falls to a fraction of normal. The market is responding by rerouting: Asian refiners are paying $8-14 premiums for US crude, and Russia is consolidating its position as the EU's second-largest LNG supplier while building Arctic and Asian alternatives ahead of the 2027 ban. The through-line is a global energy map being redrawn around chokepoint control — with the US asserting dominance over Hormuz, Gulf states building their own Red Sea security, and Russia and China deepening their Arctic energy corridor.
sources: CBS News, Yahoo News, Mathrubhumi, Reuters (via OilPrice), OilPrice.com, TASS/Eurostat, CNN, MSN, Protothema, Ilkha, ProPakistani, Morningstar/Dow Jones, Yahoo Finance, Baker Hughes
